subtopics.title: inference
subtopics.teaching: Infer meaning from explicit textual evidence plus reasonable implications. Distinguish what a passage states from what it strongly suggests, and use surrounding details to constrain interpretation.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: If a character repeatedly checks the empty station clock and watches the road, infer that the character is waiting for someone rather than merely describing the setting.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not select an inference that is merely possible; the best answer must be supported by multiple clues and should not contradict the passage.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: make evidence-based inferences, cite the clues that support them, reject unsupported interpretations, and distinguish inference from fact.

subtopics.title: author purpose
subtopics.teaching: Identify why an author chose to write a passage: to inform, explain, persuade, entertain, compare, criticize, reflect, or achieve another specific communicative goal. Use the whole passage rather than one sentence.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A passage presents statistics, addresses a common objection, and ends with a recommendation; its primary purpose is likely persuasion supported by evidence.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not confuse topic with purpose. A passage about recycling is not necessarily written merely 'about recycling'; its purpose may be to persuade readers to change behaviour.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify primary and secondary purposes, connect purpose to textual choices, and reject answers that describe only the topic.

subtopics.title: tone
subtopics.teaching: Identify tone from diction, imagery, syntax, attitude, and context. Distinguish the author's attitude toward the subject from the emotional reaction a reader might have.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Words such as 'remarkable,' 'carefully designed,' and 'promising' create an approving or optimistic tone rather than a neutral one.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not label tone from a single emotionally charged word; consider whether the passage as a whole is formal, skeptical, admiring, humorous, critical, urgent, or restrained.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: justify tone with precise language evidence, distinguish closely related tones, and explain how wording creates the identified attitude.

subtopics.title: argument structure
subtopics.teaching: Trace an argument through claim, reasons, evidence, assumptions, counterclaims, and conclusion. Determine how each part contributes to the writer's overall position.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A writer claims school gardens improve learning, supports the claim with two studies, answers a cost objection, and concludes with a recommendation; those moves form a structured argument.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat every statement as a main claim. Examples and statistics may support a claim without being the argument's central position.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: map an argument, identify supporting and opposing components, evaluate logical connections, and explain how structure strengthens or weakens the case.

subtopics.title: evidence evaluation
subtopics.teaching: Evaluate whether evidence is relevant, sufficient, credible, representative, and correctly connected to a claim. Distinguish direct evidence from anecdote, assumption, and opinion.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: One student's experience may illustrate a possibility but cannot by itself establish that an educational policy works for all students.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not equate a precise number with strong evidence. Data can still be irrelevant, biased, outdated, or interpreted beyond what it supports.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: match evidence to claims, identify weaknesses in support, recognize overgeneralization, and select the strongest evidence for a conclusion.

subtopics.title: roots
subtopics.teaching: Use common Greek and Latin roots to infer the meanings of unfamiliar English words while checking the result against context. Recognize that roots provide clues, not complete definitions.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: The root 'bio' relates to life, so 'biography' concerns a person's life; context confirms the precise meaning.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not assume every word containing similar letters shares the same root or meaning; historical spelling and borrowed forms can mislead.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify useful roots, infer plausible meanings, verify them in context, and distinguish root clues from full dictionary definitions.

subtopics.title: context precision
subtopics.teaching: Choose the vocabulary meaning that fits the exact context, register, grammatical role, and nuance of a sentence. Compare near-synonyms rather than accepting the first broadly related definition.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'economical' means avoiding waste or expense, while 'economic' relates more generally to the economy; context determines the correct choice.
subtopics.pitfall: A synonym can be broadly similar but still wrong because of connotation, collocation, register, or part of speech.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: distinguish near-synonyms, use context precisely, explain why alternatives fail, and select vocabulary appropriate to meaning and register.

subtopics.title: collocations
subtopics.teaching: Learn natural word partnerships such as 'make a decision,' 'strong evidence,' and 'deeply concerned.' Collocations are conventional combinations that fluent English tends to prefer.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Both 'strong evidence' and 'powerful evidence' may be understandable, but 'strong evidence' is the standard collocation in formal English.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not translate word combinations directly from another language or assume any grammatically possible adjective-noun pairing is equally natural.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify common collocations, complete them accurately, detect unnatural combinations, and apply them in original sentences.

subtopics.title: nuance
subtopics.teaching: Distinguish fine differences in meaning, connotation, intensity, and attitude between related words. Use context to determine which shade of meaning the writer intends.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'confident,' 'assertive,' 'arrogant,' and 'conceited' all relate to self-assurance but differ substantially in evaluation and intensity.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat near-synonyms as interchangeable when the emotional or social implication changes the message.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: compare nuanced vocabulary choices, explain connotations, rank degrees of meaning, and select wording that matches a precise communicative intention.

subtopics.title: academic vocabulary
subtopics.teaching: Interpret and use formal vocabulary common in analytical and educational writing, including terms such as analyze, infer, contrast, evaluate, significant, and consequently.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'Evaluate the evidence' asks for a judgment based on criteria and evidence, not simply a summary of what the evidence says.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not substitute everyday words automatically when a question depends on the technical distinction between academic command terms.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: understand academic command vocabulary, distinguish related terms, and apply them accurately when reading or responding.

subtopics.title: complex sentences
subtopics.teaching: Analyze complex sentences by identifying independent and dependent clauses and understanding how subordination expresses relationships such as cause, condition, contrast, and time.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In 'Although the route was longer, we arrived early because traffic was light,' the clauses express contrast and cause within one sentence.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not mistake sentence length for complexity; a long list can be simple, while a short sentence may contain meaningful subordination.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: parse complex structures, identify clause relationships, preserve meaning when rewriting, and explain punctuation choices.

subtopics.title: clauses
subtopics.teaching: Distinguish independent clauses, which can stand as complete sentences, from dependent clauses introduced by subordinators or relative markers. Identify noun, adjective, and adverb clause functions.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In 'I know that the team won,' the clause 'that the team won' functions as the object of 'know.'
subtopics.pitfall: A dependent clause may contain a subject and verb but still be incomplete in meaning or grammatical function when separated from the main clause.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify clause boundaries and types, explain their functions, and combine or separate clauses without creating fragments or faulty structures.

subtopics.title: agreement
subtopics.teaching: Apply subject-verb and pronoun-antecedent agreement by identifying the true grammatical subject rather than being distracted by nearby nouns.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'The collection of rare books is valuable' takes 'is' because 'collection' is the singular subject, not 'books.'
subtopics.pitfall: Do not match the verb to the closest noun automatically; intervening phrases and compound structures can hide the grammatical subject.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify agreement relationships in complex sentences, correct errors, and explain why the grammatical subject controls the form.

subtopics.title: modifiers
subtopics.teaching: Place modifiers close to the words they logically describe so that meaning is clear and unintended interpretations are avoided. Recognize misplaced and dangling modifiers.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'Walking through the museum, Maya noticed the sculpture' clearly makes Maya the person walking; a dangling version would wrongly suggest the sculpture was walking.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not judge a modifier only by whether the sentence sounds familiar; check who or what the modifier logically describes.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify modifier errors, repair ambiguous constructions, and explain how placement changes meaning.

subtopics.title: tense consistency
subtopics.teaching: Maintain logical tense relationships across a passage while allowing deliberate shifts for changes in time, reported speech, or general truths.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'She entered the room and noticed that the lights were off' uses past forms consistently for linked past events.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not force every verb into the same tense when the time relationship genuinely changes; consistency means logical alignment, not mechanical uniformity.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify unjustified tense shifts, preserve intended time relationships, and edit paragraphs for coherent tense use.

subtopics.title: error identification
subtopics.teaching: Edit systematically for grammar, usage, word choice, punctuation, agreement, tense, and sentence structure. Read the complete sentence before deciding which segment contains the error.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: In 'Neither of the answers are correct,' identify the singular subject 'neither' and correct the verb to 'is.'
subtopics.pitfall: Do not select an error simply because a phrase sounds unusual; verify it against the grammatical rule and the intended meaning.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: locate errors efficiently, name the underlying rule, distinguish real errors from acceptable variation, and produce a corrected sentence.

subtopics.title: sentence transformation
subtopics.teaching: Transform sentences while preserving their essential meaning, tense, logical relationships, and required grammatical information. Common transformations include active/passive, direct/indirect speech, joining clauses, and changing degree or structure.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: 'People speak English worldwide' can become 'English is spoken worldwide' without changing the core proposition.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not change tense, emphasis, negation, or meaning accidentally while altering the grammatical form.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: perform multiple transformation types accurately, preserve meaning, and explain the grammatical changes made.

subtopics.title: punctuation
subtopics.teaching: Use punctuation to clarify sentence boundaries, relationships, lists, quotations, and emphasis. Understand the functions of commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, quotation marks, and dashes.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: A semicolon can join closely related independent clauses when no coordinating conjunction is used; a colon can introduce an explanation or list after a complete clause.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not use commas simply where a reader might pause. Punctuation follows grammatical structure as well as rhythm and style.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: correct punctuation in complex sentences, explain each mark's function, and distinguish grammatical necessity from optional stylistic punctuation.

subtopics.title: style
subtopics.teaching: Analyze style as the combined effect of diction, sentence structure, imagery, formality, rhythm, and rhetorical choices. Style should be described with evidence rather than vague labels.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: Short sentences, direct verbs, and concrete nouns can create a brisk, accessible style, while longer periodic sentences and formal diction can create a reflective or academic style.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not confuse style with tone. Tone is the writer's attitude; style is the characteristic way that attitude and ideas are expressed.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify distinctive stylistic features, connect them to textual effects, compare styles across passages, and support judgments with precise evidence.

subtopics.title: passage editing
subtopics.teaching: Edit a complete passage by checking meaning, grammar, cohesion, word choice, punctuation, and consistency together. Read beyond individual sentences so that corrections improve the passage as a whole.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: When editing a paragraph, first locate the main idea and sentence relationships, then correct agreement and punctuation, remove repetition, and replace vague wording without changing the intended message.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not correct every unusual expression automatically; some variation is intentional. An edit is valid when it improves correctness or clarity while preserving meaning and context.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: edit multi-sentence passages accurately, prioritize errors, preserve the writer's intended meaning, and explain the rule or clarity improvement behind each major correction.

subtopics.title: theme
subtopics.teaching: Master theme within Literature for National English Championship. Establish the underlying rule or algorithm, trace representative cases, analyse edge conditions, and practise transfer to unfamiliar competition problems. Students should justify the method, identify why plausible alternatives fail, and verify the result rather than relying on pattern matching alone.

subtopics.mastery: Mastery: independently solve an unfamiliar precision checking problem, explain the method, handle an edge case, reject a plausible wrong approach, and verify the final answer or output.

subtopics.title: mixed language sets
subtopics.teaching: Master mixed language sets within Championship Language Strategy for National English Championship. Establish the underlying rule or algorithm, trace representative cases, analyse edge conditions, and practise transfer to unfamiliar competition problems. Students should justify the method, identify why plausible alternatives fail, and verify the result rather than relying on pattern matching alone.
